question_type: Arithmetic mean of a year-end bank-reported liabilities series (total foreign countries, all liability types) over six calendar years

opus_divergence.what_opus_did: Picked the right table and column (CM-I-2 'Total Liabilities by Type, Payable in Dollars', Part A 'Foreign Countries', column (1) 'Total foreign countries', year-end rows). Opus scanned every vintage and saw that the 1995 value was revised slightly and the Dec 1996 value, printed as preliminary ('p') in the March 1997 issue, was revised about 2.4% higher from March 1998 on and then stayed the same. It still took all six values from the March 1997 issue, because that is the only issue whose table covers exactly 1991-1996 (the 'the asked range matches one printed table' heuristic). It computed the latest-revision mean as an alternative and rejected it.
opus_divergence.what_right_glm_did: cards used the same table and column but followed a latest-revision-per-year rule. It read CM-I-2 Part A in the 1996_12 through 1998_03 issues and took each year from the latest issue it found carrying that year. The early years come from the March 1997 table and the Dec 1996 value comes from the revised ('r') March 1998 printing, so the values are stitched from several issues.
opus_divergence.evidence: Opus worklog.md:27 (single-issue conclusion), worklog.md:45 and calc.py:43-46 (latest-revision mean computed, then kept only as an alternative), solution.json:50-57 (vintage decision 'March 1997 issue'), solution.json:68 (alternatives); cards [9] ('revisions likely annual data revised in later issues'), [22] ('Need latest revisions'), [25]-[31] (located and read CM-I-2 Part A across 1996-1998 issues), [32]-[33] (latest value per year, mean)

reviewer_flag: Verdict 'confirmed' (review.json). The reviewer re-scanned CM-I-2 Part A in 1997_03-2002_12 and named the latest-revision vintage as residual risk (b). It still endorsed the single-issue reading because 'the exact 1991-1996 span matches the Mar 1997 table' (review.md:13, 18).
right_by_principled_choice_or_luck: Mostly principled. At [9] cards said it would use the latest revision, by analogy to card C003 (a 'take the latest issue printing the year' rule written for agency outlays, not for this table), and it repeated this at [22]. It then compared several printings ([29]-[31]) and took the latest. There was some luck: for Dec 1996 it stopped checking at the 1998_03 issue. Opus's scan shows the value did not change after that, so the shortcut happened to be safe.
wrong_glm_arms_same_as_opus: none arm: yes, exactly the same choice. It used the same table and the same March 1997 single-issue vintage because 'CM-I-2 ... has all years 1991-1996 in Mar 1997' ([51], [56], [66]). After weighing latest revisions at [49] it chose the single table, and its answer, like Opus's, is within 1% of the reference. prompt arm: no. It applied the latest-vintage rule like cards ([21], guided by its procedure step 1 'compare it with the latest bulletin carrying the same row'). It went wrong by choosing a different series: the CM-I-3 / CM-I-1 foreign-countries total, which also counts liabilities payable in foreign currencies ([35], [47]-[66]). Its error is SOURCE_TABLE, not vintage.
lesson_for_harness: Opus used the heuristic 'one printed table spans exactly the asked years, so take every value from that issue'. That heuristic is wrong when the question pins no date. The reference follows the latest revision of each value even when that means stitching issues together, which matches the benchmark paper's stated convention (most up-to-date revision unless the question pins a date). The vintage rule should be a default applied to each value: grep each row forward, take the latest printing, and prefer 'r' over 'p'. A coincidence between the asked range and one table must not override it. Both adapter arms that carried a latest-vintage rule (cards via the C003 analogy, prompt via its procedure text and L-cmi1-annual-vintage) applied it; Opus and the no-adapter arm did not. A CHECK that flags any cited cell marked 'p' (preliminary), or any cell that a later printing supersedes, would have caught Opus's choice mechanically.
notes: The two vintages differ by only about 0.5% on the mean. Almost all of the gap comes from the preliminary Dec 1996 cell, plus a negligible 1995 revision, but exact-match grading makes it decisive. Opus computed the correct-vintage number itself and rejected it, so this was a decision-rule error, not a search failure. The prompt arm's table mistake is the one that its later lesson L-cmi2-partA-total-foreign-countries (visible in the Q37 context) was written to fix.
